q: Each C5H8 diene below is hydrogenated to pentane with 2 equiv H2/Pt. Which one releases the least heat (smallest |ΔH°hydrog|)?
h: All four give the same product, so the least heat comes from the most stable starting diene. Think conjugation first, then sterics.
w: Because every isomer ends at pentane, the most stable diene has the smallest heat of hydrogenation. Conjugated dienes are stabilized by π overlap across the central C2–C3 bond (and a stronger sp2–sp2 σ bond), and the E isomer avoids the steric clash of the Z isomer. So (E)-1,3-pentadiene releases the least heat (about −226 kJ/mol, versus about −254 kJ/mol for 1,4-pentadiene and nearly −300 kJ/mol for the allene).
x: 1,4-Pentadiene has two isolated C=C bonds with no delocalization, so it releases more heat than a conjugated isomer.
1,2-Pentadiene is a cumulated diene (allene); its sp central carbon makes it the least stable isomer, so it releases the most heat.
(Z)-1,3-Pentadiene is conjugated, but its methyl crowds the C3 hydrogen, so it is slightly less stable than the E isomer and releases a little more heat.

q: Use the heats of hydrogenation in the table to estimate the extra stabilization (delocalization energy) of 1,3-butadiene relative to a hypothetical diene with two isolated monosubstituted C=C bonds.
h: Two isolated C=C bonds would each release about the same heat as one 1-butene. Compare that sum with the measured value.
w: Two isolated monosubstituted C=C bonds would release about 2 × (−127) = −254 kJ/mol. Butadiene releases only −237 kJ/mol, so it starts 254 − 237 = about 17 kJ/mol lower in energy (more stable). That difference is the conjugation (delocalization) energy.
x: Less heat released means the diene started lower in energy, so it is more stable, not less.
110 kJ/mol is the difference between butadiene and a single 1-butene (237 − 127), which compares one C=C with two.
127 kJ/mol is just the heat of hydrogenation of one C=C; it is not a stabilization energy.

q:
Which statements about cumulated dienes (allenes) are correct?
I. The central carbon of an allene is sp hybridized.
II. The two π bonds of an allene lie in perpendicular planes.
III. 2,3-Pentadiene (CH3CH=C=CHCH3) is chiral even though it has no stereocenter.
IV. Among C5H8 diene isomers, allenes have the smallest heats of hydrogenation.
h: Picture the central carbon using one p orbital for each π bond. What does that do to the planes of the two end groups?
w: The central allene carbon forms two π bonds with two different p orbitals, so it is sp (I true) and the two π bonds are perpendicular (II true). That puts the H/CH3 pair on one end in a plane perpendicular to the pair on the other end, so CH3CH=C=CHCH3 has no mirror plane and is chiral (axial chirality, III true). Allenes are the least stable dienes and have the largest heats of hydrogenation, so IV is false. Answer: I, II and III only.
x: Statement III is also true: the perpendicular end groups make 2,3-pentadiene a chiral molecule with a chiral axis.
Statement II is omitted and IV is false: allenes release the most heat on hydrogenation, not the least.
Statement I is true and IV is false; cumulated dienes are less stable than both isolated and conjugated dienes.

q: 1,3-Butadiene reacts with 1 equiv of HBr at −80 °C. Which is the major product?
h: Protonate a terminal carbon to make an allylic cation. At low temperature the product that forms fastest wins.
w: H+ adds to C1, giving an allylic cation with positive character on C2 and C4. At −80 °C the addition is irreversible, so the product that forms fastest dominates: bromide attacks C2, which is right next to it in the ion pair and carries more of the positive charge (secondary). The kinetic 1,2-product 3-bromo-1-butene is major.
x: 1-Bromo-2-butene is the 1,4-product; it is more stable but forms more slowly, so it is major only when the reaction can equilibrate at higher temperature.
4-Bromo-1-butene would need protonation at C2 to give a primary, non-allylic cation (or a radical anti-Markovnikov path); neither happens here.
2-Bromo-1-butene has Br on an sp<sup>2</sup> (vinylic) carbon; capture of the allylic cation always puts Br on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon.

q: The same HBr addition to 1,3-butadiene is run at 40 °C and allowed to reach equilibrium. Which statement best describes the outcome?
c: Mostly 1-bromo-2-butene, because the products interconvert and it has the more substituted, more stable C=C
Mostly 3-bromo-1-butene, because attack at C2 has the lower activation energy
Mostly 1-bromo-2-butene, because attack at C4 has the lower activation energy
About 1:1, because both products come from the same allylic cation
h: At higher temperature the products can re-ionize. When that happens, which property of a product decides how much of it you get?
w: At 40 °C the C–Br bonds re-ionize back to the allylic cation, so the system reaches equilibrium (thermodynamic control). The product ratio then reflects product stability, and 1-bromo-2-butene, with a disubstituted internal C=C, is the major product. The 1,2-product still forms faster, but it keeps reverting.
x: Lower activation energy explains the low-temperature (kinetic) result; under equilibrium the faster-forming product is not the one that accumulates.
The 1,4-product is major for the right reason only if you cite stability; attack at C4 actually has the higher barrier.
A shared intermediate does not force equal amounts: the two paths have different barriers and the two products have different stabilities.

q: The energy diagram shows 1,3-butadiene + HBr → 3-bromo-1-butene. Which statement is correct?
c: B is the allylic carbocation, and the step through A is rate-determining
A is the allylic carbocation, and the step through C is rate-determining
B is a transition state in which the C–H bond is partly formed
C is the highest point, so bromide attack is rate-determining
h: Maxima are transition states and minima between them are intermediates. The rate-determining step has the highest transition state.
w: Minima between two maxima are intermediates, so B is the allylic carbocation. A is the transition state for protonation of the diene and C is the transition state for bromide attack. A is the highest point on the path, so protonation (through A) is rate-determining; bromide capture of the cation is fast.
x: A is a maximum, so it is a transition state, not an intermediate; and C is lower than A.
B is a minimum, so it is an intermediate (the cation), not a transition state.
C is lower than A in the diagram, so the bromide-attack step is not rate-determining.

q: The table gives free energies (kJ/mol) relative to the allylic cation + Br<sup>−</sup> formed from 1,3-butadiene and HBr. On warming, the 1,2-product gradually converts into the 1,4-product. Which explanation is consistent with these data?
c: The 1,2-product re-ionizes over a 49 kJ/mol barrier, smaller than the 61 kJ/mol barrier for the 1,4-product, so material drains into the more stable 1,4-product
The 1,4-product forms over a smaller barrier (13 kJ/mol) than the 1,2-product (9 kJ/mol), so it is favored at all temperatures
The 1,2-product rearranges directly to the 1,4-product by a 1,3-shift of Br without forming the cation
The 1,2-product re-ionizes over a 9 kJ/mol barrier, so it is never formed at any temperature
h: For each product, calculate the barrier to go back up to its transition state. Which product escapes more easily, and which one traps the material?
w: Reverse barriers: 1,2-product → cation, 9 − (−40) = 49 kJ/mol; 1,4-product → cation, 13 − (−48) = 61 kJ/mol. When warmed enough to cross these barriers, the 1,2-product returns to the cation much more often than the 1,4-product does, and each return gives another chance to form the 1,4-product. Material therefore drains into the more stable 1,4-product (lower G, larger reverse barrier), the thermodynamic product. At low temperature the 4 kJ/mol difference in forward barriers (9 vs 13) makes the 1,2-product the kinetic product.
x: 13 kJ/mol is the larger forward barrier, not the smaller; the 1,4-product forms more slowly, so it cannot be favored at all temperatures.
The data describe a path through the allylic cation; the interconversion is ionization and recombination, not a direct Br shift.
9 kJ/mol is the forward barrier from the cation; the 1,2-product is the major product at low temperature.

q: Isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene) reacts with 1 equiv of HBr at −78 °C (kinetic control). Which is the major 1,2-addition (kinetic) product?
h: Compare the two terminal carbons you could protonate. Which choice gives an allylic cation that is also tertiary? Then decide 1,2 vs 1,4.
w: Protonating C1 (the CH2 next to the methyl-bearing carbon) gives an allylic cation whose positive charge is shared by a tertiary carbon (C2) and a primary carbon (C4). Protonating C4 instead gives a secondary/primary allylic cation, which is less stable. At −78 °C bromide traps the cation fastest at the carbon with the most positive charge, next to it in the ion pair, so the kinetic 1,2-product is 3-bromo-3-methyl-1-butene.
x: 1-Bromo-3-methyl-2-butene is the 1,4-product, with a trisubstituted C=C; it is the thermodynamic product seen at higher temperature.
3-Bromo-2-methyl-1-butene comes from protonating the other terminal carbon, which makes a less stable secondary allylic cation.
4-Bromo-2-methyl-1-butene is an anti-Markovnikov product that would need a radical (HBr/ROOR) mechanism.

q: 1,3-Cyclohexadiene is treated with 1 equiv of HBr. How many constitutional isomers are obtained as products?
h: Draw the allylic cation formed by protonating C1, add Br at each cationic carbon, and number both products from scratch.
w: Protonating C1 gives an allylic cation with positive charge on C2 and C4 (double bond C3=C4 ↔ C2=C3). Bromide at C2 leaves C3=C4: Br is on the carbon next to the C=C. Bromide at C4 leaves C2=C3: Br is again on the carbon next to the C=C. Because the ring makes the two ends equivalent, both are 3-bromocyclohexene (one constitutional isomer) (formed as a racemate).
x: 4-Bromocyclohexene would need Br two carbons from the C=C; neither cationic carbon is in that position.
1-Bromocyclohexene has Br on a vinylic carbon, which no step of this mechanism produces.
Only one constitutional product forms; the 4-bromo and 1-bromo isomers are not reachable from the allylic cation.

q: In the carbocation shown, which labeled carbons share the positive charge?
h: Draw the second resonance form by moving the π electrons toward the cationic carbon.
w: Shifting the Ca=Cb π electrons toward Cc gives the resonance form CH3CH+–CH=CH2. The charge alternates, so it is shared by the two end carbons, a and c; the central carbon b carries none. The form with the charge on a (secondary) contributes more.
x: The charge is delocalized; ignoring resonance leaves it only on c.
In an allylic system the central carbon never carries the positive charge in any resonance form.
Carbon b is a node of the allyl nonbonding orbital, so it bears no positive charge.

q: Which alkene gives only one constitutional isomer of monobromide when treated with NBS and light (ignore stereoisomers)?
h: Find every allylic hydrogen, form each allylic radical, and draw both resonance forms. Count distinct bromides.
w: NBS/hν abstracts an allylic H to give a resonance-stabilized allylic radical, and Br can attach at either end. In cyclohexene both allylic CH2 groups are equivalent and the two ends of the allylic radical are equivalent, so the only product is 3-bromocyclohexene (racemic).
x: 1-Butene gives an allylic radical with unequal ends, so 3-bromo-1-butene and 1-bromo-2-butene both form.
(E)-2-Pentene has two different allylic positions (C1 and C4), and each radical has two different ends, giving several bromides.
1-Methylcyclohexene has three different allylic positions (CH<sub>3</sub>, C3 and C6), giving a mixture of constitutional isomers.

q: In the allyl radical (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>•), where is the unpaired electron found, according to π MO theory?
c: In ψ<sub>2</sub>, a nonbonding MO with a node at C2, so the spin is on C1 and C3
In ψ<sub>1</sub>, a bonding MO spread evenly over all three carbons
In ψ<sub>2</sub>, a nonbonding MO concentrated on C2
In ψ<sub>3</sub>, an antibonding MO with nodes between each pair of carbons
h: Three p orbitals give three MOs. Fill three electrons from the bottom and look at the shape of the singly occupied one.
w: Three p orbitals combine to give ψ1 (bonding, 0 nodes), ψ2 (nonbonding, 1 node) and ψ3 (antibonding, 2 nodes). Three π electrons fill ψ1 twice and ψ2 once. The node of ψ2 passes through C2, so the unpaired electron is in ψ2 and resides on C1 and C3, matching the two resonance forms.
x: ψ<sub>1</sub> holds two paired electrons; the third electron must go into the next orbital.
ψ2 has its node at C2, so it has zero coefficient there, not a concentration.
ψ<sub>3</sub> is empty in the radical; it would only be occupied in an excited state.

q: How many nodes (perpendicular to the carbon chain, not counting the molecular plane) does ψ<sub>3</sub> of 1,3-butadiene have?
h: In a linear π system, ψ<sub>n</sub> has n − 1 nodes.
w: For a linear conjugated system, the number of nodes grows by one per MO: ψ1 0, ψ2 1, ψ3 2, ψ4 3. ψ3 (the LUMO of ground-state butadiene) has 2 nodes.
x: One node is ψ<sub>2</sub>, the HOMO of butadiene.
Three nodes is ψ<sub>4</sub>, the highest antibonding MO.
Zero nodes is ψ<sub>1</sub>, the lowest bonding MO.

q: 1,3,5-Hexatriene absorbs UV light, promoting one electron from the HOMO to the LUMO. In this excited state, which MO is the highest occupied orbital, and how many nodes does it have?
h: Six π electrons fill ψ<sub>1</sub>–ψ<sub>3</sub> in the ground state. Move one electron up one level.
w: Six p orbitals give ψ1–ψ6. In the ground state six electrons fill ψ1–ψ3, so the HOMO is ψ3 (2 nodes) and the LUMO is ψ4. After excitation one electron sits in ψ4, so the highest occupied MO is ψ4, with 3 nodes. This is why photochemical electrocyclic reactions follow the opposite rotation to thermal ones.
x: ψ<sub>3</sub> with 2 nodes is the ground-state HOMO, before excitation.
ψ<sub>4</sub> is correct, but it has n − 1 = 3 nodes, not 4.
ψ<sub>5</sub> is empty in both the ground state and the first excited state.

q: Which compound has the longest-wavelength UV absorption (largest λ<sub>max</sub>)?
h: More conjugated π bonds in a row mean a smaller HOMO–LUMO gap.
w: Each added conjugated C=C raises the HOMO and lowers the LUMO, shrinking the gap, so absorption moves to longer wavelength (lower energy). 1,3,5,7-Octatetraene, with four conjugated C=C bonds, has the largest λmax (near 290 nm) compared with hexatriene (about 258 nm) and butadiene (217 nm).
x: 1,3,5-Hexatriene has three conjugated C=C bonds, one fewer than octatetraene, so its gap is larger.
1,3-Butadiene has only two conjugated C=C bonds; it absorbs near 217 nm.
1,5-Hexadiene has isolated C=C bonds, so it absorbs below 200 nm like a simple alkene.

q: Rank compounds I–III by λ<sub>max</sub> in the UV spectrum, from shortest to longest wavelength.
h: Count how many C=C bonds are conjugated with each other in each compound; isolated bonds do not count together.
w: λmax increases as the HOMO–LUMO gap shrinks with longer conjugation. I (1,4-pentadiene) has isolated C=C bonds and absorbs below 200 nm; II (1,3-pentadiene) is a conjugated diene (about 223 nm); III (2,4,6-octatriene) is a conjugated triene (above 260 nm). So I < II < III.
x: Two isolated C=C bonds do not act like a diene; I absorbs at shorter wavelength than the conjugated diene II.
This is the order by energy of absorption, not wavelength; the longest conjugation absorbs at the longest wavelength.
The triene III has the longest conjugation, so it absorbs at a longer wavelength than the diene II.

q: Isomers X and Y both have formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub> and both take up 2 equiv of H<sub>2</sub> to give hexane. X absorbs at 227 nm; Y shows no absorption above 200 nm. Which pair fits?
h: Absorption near 220–230 nm signals a conjugated diene. Also check that Y gives hexane with 2 equiv of H<sub>2</sub>.
w: A λmax above 200 nm needs conjugation, so X is a conjugated diene: (E)-2,4-hexadiene fits (about 227 nm). Y has two C=C bonds (2 H2 → hexane, so no ring) but no conjugation, so it is an isolated diene such as 1,5-hexadiene. Answer: X = (E)-2,4-hexadiene; Y = 1,5-hexadiene.
x: This reverses the assignment: the conjugated diene is the one that absorbs at 227 nm.
1,4-Hexadiene is an isolated diene, so it would not absorb at 227 nm.
Cyclohexene takes up only 1 equiv of H<sub>2</sub> and gives cyclohexane, not hexane.
